entries.title: The Best Labor Day Mattress Deals on Beds We’ve Tried in Our Homes
entries.summary: It’s one of the best times of the year to buy a mattress, and our top tested picks are on sale.
entries.content:
Mattress deals come around pretty frequently, which means you can almost always save at least some money. But the very best deals come around Memorial Day, Labor Day, Black Friday, and Cyber Monday. If you're in the market for a new bed, or you need some sleep accessories like bedding, pillows, or blankets, we've found deals on tried-and-tested favorites. We'll update this story again as more Labor Day mattress deals go live.

Be sure to check out our related roundups for deals on tools, outdoor gear, tech, and kitchen goods.

WIRED Featured Mattress Deals

Early Labor Day Mattress Deals

Use code LUXE25 at checkout to save on the best mattress we've ever tried. Out of the hundreds of options we tested, this strikes the best balance between features and price for most sleepers. Individually wrapped springs provide support and pressure relief, and six layers of cushioning mean it's cozy but not overly plush. Make sure you get deep-pocketed sheets to accommodate the 13-inch height.

The best hybrid mattress has a fabric cover that helps to wick away and disperse your body heat. If you're a hot sleeper, it can help alleviate your problems. And it can help with back pain as well, thanks to its different types of coils arranged into three strategic zones. The pillowtop can make the mattress feel softer than you might expect, so keep that in mind when you're choosing between the three firmness levels.

The best mattress for side sleepers has been a personal favorite among WIRED reviewers. It offers enough support to keep side sleepers' spines aligned without pushing things out of whack. This bed is bouncy and temperature-neutral, though you can pay a bit more for a cooling pillowtop that will decrease the mattress's firmness.

This affordable mattress is even more accessibly priced for Labor Day. It's a little firm, but offers great contouring and pressure relief, and motion stays isolated. The bed also doesn't get too hot overnight. If you prefer a slightly softer bed, you might want to pair this one with a mattress topper.

We quite like this inexpensive mattress. It's literally cool to the touch and therefore ideal for hot sleepers. And while you might think of cooling beds as being more suited to summer, they can also be nice in winter, since they'll help prevent you from overheating under all those covers. It's available in three firmness levels—we think the softest would be too soft.

Our top firm pick for back pain is still fine for side sleepers. It's very firm, with five layers of foam and coils, so it might be a bit shocking at first. But the support will help prevent and possibly even alleviate sore spots and back pain, and it's a particularly good pick for couples where one person might crave additional support for their spine while sleeping. The phase change material helps keep you cool.

Early Labor Day Bedding and Accessory Deals

These bamboo sheets are a must-have, per resident sheet expert Nena Farrell. They're silky, soft, and cozy, with a supremely comfortable and lightweight drape. They'll make you feel sleepy right away and get even softer over time. We also like the color selection.

This is my favorite down comforter. I keep it on my bed as soon as it starts getting a little chilly out. It's fluffy and lofty, but still well ventilated, and the construction of the baffle boxes and down-proof fabric means I'm never getting stabbed with a feather in my sleep. It feels very cloud-like and is available in three warmth levels.

Our favorite mattress topper is organic. It's made with cotton and latex, so it's soft but still slightly springy and supportive. It's nice and plush but won't turn your bed into something too squishy or cradling. While it doesn't have straps, it's heavy enough to stay put.

entries.title: Best Early Tech Labor Day Sales I’d Shop Myself (2026): AirTags, Dyson, and More
entries.summary: From the best Dyson vacuum to the best wireless earbuds we’ve tested, you can get some great gadgets on sale already ahead of Labor Day.
entries.content:
It's never too early for deals, and the sales have already started popping up for Labor Day. While the holiday is a little later than usual this year (falling on Monday, September 7), that hasn't stopped plenty of our favorite tech gear from going on sale, from Dyson vacuums to Apple AirTags.

Every item we feature is a tech gadget the WIRED Reviews team has tested and loved, usually a top pick from our guides, ranging from headphones and speakers to vacuums and chargers. We'll be keeping an eye on the sales leading up to and through the holiday, so don't miss your chance to get something off your tech wish list for a better price with these Labor Day sales.

Updated August 31: We've ensured accuracy throughout, removed expired deals, and added new discounts on Nothing earbuds, the JBL Clip 5, a magnetic car mount, a fan, the Sony XM5 headphones, a Soundcore speaker, and a robot vacuum. Louryn Strampe also contributed to this story.

WIRED Featured Tech Deals

Early Gadget Deals for Labor Day

Need an AirTag to track your keys or luggage (or in my case, my son's backpack when we're on a trip)? Apple's line of Bluetooth trackers can add up if you need to buy a lot, but you can get $5 off a single one right now, or $10 off a four-pack.

If you're a Google Pixel user and you need a new case, Dbrand makes one of our favorite cases for Pixel phones—especially if you're in the market for a clear one. Its Pixelsnap-certified magnets are strong, the edges around the camera are slightly raised for extra protection, and it's grippy. There's no plasticky texture, either, which is nice to find on a clear case.

This charging tray from Courant is, simply put, gorgeous. It comes in both leather and linen finishes, and there are two chargers built into it for your phone and your wireless earbuds. The left charger is MagSafe-compatible, while the right side is a Qi charger you can use with either Apple or non-Apple products.

The best MagSafe car mount is usually pretty affordable, but this discount makes it even more attainable. It's well ventilated and sticks supremely to any flat surface. It's compatible with any MagSafe phone (or any magnetic phone case, which yours should be regardless of operating system.)

This smart tower fan is an honorable mention in our buying guide with the caveat that we like it more when it goes on sale. Well, it's on sale right now, coming within $5 of the lowest price we've tracked. It's quiet and tall, with a neat hidden digital display.

Early Vacuum Sales for Labor Day

My personal standout from Dyson's newest vacuum is the V10 Konical. It has the new Dyson vacuum head, the All Floor Cones, and is usually on sale for the same price as the V8 Cyclone. However, the V10 Konical did better in my testing. While the base vacuum isn't on sale right now, the version with the Auto-empty Dok is. That means you can get a great all-around Dyson that's already well-priced, plus a docking station that both empties and charges the vacuum.

Our top robot vacuum is down to the second-best deal we've seen, and it regularly jumps back up to its full $1,400 price. If you're in the market and don't want to wait until fall shopping events like Prime Day or Black Friday, this is a safe buy for a great gadget. Built-in AI intelligently cleans tricky messes, and the extendable arm can reach places other vacuums can't. It also empties its own dust bin when cleaning is done, and it can even lift itself out of a situation when it gets stuck (most of the time).

Early Speaker and Headphone Deals for Labor Day

The best Bluetooth speaker is the JBL Flip 7, and it's on sale for a little more than $50 off ahead of Labor Day. Buying a portable Bluetooth speaker means you won't get everything you'd look for in a speaker, but the Flip 7 has a good balance between mobility and sound quality. It also packs better water resistance than past Flip models and a two-hour battery (or four with reduced bass). Not every color is on sale for this low, but most are at least slightly discounted.

This clip-on speaker packs surprisingly chunky sound for its size. The built-in carabiner means you can easily tote it around while you're on the go, and the onboard controls are easy to find and operate. This deal is solidly in the middle of what we tend to see; sometimes it falls a bit more in price, but this discount isn't a bad one.

This speaker fluctuates in price very often, and it has remained a steadfast budget recommendation in our Bluetooth speaker buying guide. We don't see it fall below $30 frequently. The sound will not blow you away. But for the price, it's decent, with great battery life and a very portable water-resistant design.

If you're in the market for a new Sonos speaker, the Move 2 has a nice discount right now with $100 off. It's a large portable speaker that's great for anyone who wants to add more punch to their Bluetooth tunes. The Move 2 has Bluetooth for streaming music on the go, Wi-Fi, and a USB-C port that can double as an analog line-in if you have a separate adapter.

They're not the newest Sony headphones we love (the XM6), but at this price, it's hard not to want to spring for it. This is the lowest price it tends to fall to, but it was selling for almost $50 more just a few days ago. Don't get me wrong—the XM6 that came out earlier this year are a significant upgrade, but if you want a beautiful-sounding, comfortable, and stylish pair of noise-canceling headphones, the Sony XM5 will still make you very happy. Especially at this price.

Nothing earbuds consistently earn mentions in our buying guides, and the latest iteration is an honorable mention being sold at a very compelling price. The Nothing Ear (3a) are stylish and have solid sound, intuitive controls, and an optional app that's actually useful. Noise cancellation could be better, but for less than $100 these are still a stellar budget pick.

entries.title: Asus ProArt 27 QD-OLED (PA279cdv) Review: HDR for All
entries.summary: I wouldn’t call it cheap, but this monitor from Asus brings proper HDR-capable video editing to creators who couldn’t previously afford an OLED display.
entries.content:
I wouldn’t call it cheap, but this monitor from Asus brings proper HDR-capable video editing to creators who couldn’t previously afford an OLED display.

Attractive, thin design. Stand comes with lots of adjustability. Forward-facing buttons are convenient. Solid HDR performance for the price. 120-Hz refresh rate is a nice bonus. Great port selection.

TIRED

Not very bright in SDR. Some quirks when connected to macOS.

OLED is common in gaming monitors these days. But for those of us who don’t need gaming gear? Well, home-office and content-creation monitors have been much slower to adopt the exciting and more capable display technology. That’s unfortunate because having an OLED monitor is every bit as useful as having an OLED TV if you ever use your monitor for entertainment purposes. OLED displays are also helpful for photo editors, videographers, game developers, and other creators who might want to work in high dynamic range (HDR) for a broader range of brightness, contrast, and color.

The PA279CDV is Asus’ attempt to bring that OLED goodness to a wider demographic, at a retail price of $699, which is competitive for the technology. This monitor makes a few compromises to hit that price, but it does so without losing what makes owning a high-end OLED display feel unique.

Unique, Ergonomic, and Easy to Use

Asus is one of the few manufacturers releasing OLED monitors precisely for this non-gamer demographic, and the PA279CDV is the cheapest it's ever had in its lineup. In fact, the monitor only has one major competitor: the Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED (9/10 WIRED Recommends). The main difference between the two is the size. Dell’s model is 31.6 inches, compared to Asus’ 27 inches. Being larger gives you more screen to work with, but it's also less sharp and takes up more desk space. The Samsung 32-inch Smart Monitor M90SF (7/10 WIRED Recommends) is the only other non-gaming OLED monitor option, but that's far more expensive.

As far as the Asus’ appearance goes, the side bezels are a bit large, and the top and bottom bezels aren’t the same size, which I find visually off-putting. Nicely, though, the amount of adjustability is impressive. This stand can swivel, tilt, rotate into portrait mode, and the height can shift 5 inches. The stand has some very basic built-in cable management, with down-firing ports that help keep cords organized. Also, the flat base doesn't require much space on my desk.

Each of the two back USB-C ports has a specific purpose. One is USB-C 3.2 with DP Alt Mode, which provides 96 watts of power delivery for your laptop. The other is a USB-C 3.2 port for the KVM switch, enabling you to connect two PCs to the monitor and switch between them seamlessly. Fortunately, Asus clearly labels each port, so you know which to use for your intended purpose. The monitor also comes with two USB-A ports for accessories, a headphone jack, HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, and a DisplayPort Out for daisy-chaining monitors together. This is a solid array of port selection that gives you just about everything you need to use the ProArt PA279cdv as a workstation.

Meanwhile, the controls for the onscreen display and menu are on the right side of the front panel. I tend to prefer just a single joystick for simplicity's sake, but like the other Asus ProArt monitors, this one gives you five control buttons, plus a power button, in addition to a joystick. Once you know how to use it, though, the buttons give you quick access to switching inputs or changing brightness.

There are quite a lot of features to dig through in the menu, including a number of color modes and detailed picture-quality tweaks. There's also a Display Widget app to handle all these settings, available in Windows 11 or macOS.

The monitor includes speakers, but they sound pretty bad, which is unfortunate for a monitor designed at least partially for entertainment purposes. Keep this in mind if you plan to watch a movie on the monitor, since you’ll only want to use the speakers for basic notifications. By contrast, the Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED has a really nice set of speakers.

OLED, Oh My!

Brightness—both measured in standard dynamic range (SDR) and HDR content—is the key feature of an OLED monitor, as it determines how good at HDR the device in question truly is. OLED displays can switch off individual pixels, a capability that provides the absolute blacks this class of display is known for. But if the pixels aren't bright enough, the display still won’t produce a strong HDR performance.

Using an HDR test pattern, I was able to record 1,038 nits in a 1 percent window and 917 nits in a 4 percent window. These strong results deliver a greater sense of visual fidelity when watching movies or playing games than what you’d get with dimmer displays. Compared to the current ultimate HDR monitor, the Apple Studio Display XDR (7/10, WIRED Recommends), though, these results aren’t stunning. On the Apple monitor, I got to 1,905 nits of brightness in a 25 percent window. Even so, comparing these two monitors is hardly fair, given that the Apple costs more than $3,000 and should provide a premium quality to match. I’m providing these results to demonstrate the broad HDR landscape in monitors.

I tested the Asus visuals in a few scenarios, including HDR video test footage, Netflix streaming, and some games. Dark scenes in Cyberpunk 2077 really come to life, aided by the deep blacks and brighter highlights. The effect isn't mind-blowing, but it's definitely noticeable.

In SDR content, though—which is where you’ll spend most of your time—the results are even less stellar. According to my meter, it maxed out in SDR at 240 nits at full-screen brightness. While that's bright enough for most days, if you sit next to a window, you might find yourself wishing for an extra 100 nits. The Dell 32 Plus 4K QD-OLED has the same issue. The good news is that while the PA279CDV has a glossy display, it’s surprisingly good at resisting reflections and glare.

I also tested the color performance, as that's one of the features that Asus claims distinguishes the PA279CDV from its more expensive OLED options, such as the ProArt PA27ucdmr ($1,401). The color gamut was fantastic across the board, meaning the panel is capable of producing great color, covering 91 percent of Adobe RGB and 98 percent in Display P3. When plugged into a Windows machine, the Spyder Pro I used measured excellent color accuracy as well—far beyond what Asus claimed.

However, when plugged into a MacBook Pro, I was unable to get that same color accuracy. For whatever reason, the best I could measure was a Delta-E of around 2.0. That's not terrible, but it's not quite pro-level. Speaking of Mac compatibility, the PA279CDV has a number of features to entice Mac users. Once you install the Display Widget app, it'll match up color temperature with your MacBook and even allow you to control screen brightness from your keyboard. (It can’t control volume, though, which is a miss.) A lot of this is very similar to what BenQ offers in its own Mac-focused line of monitors, such as the BenQ 5K MA270S that I recently tested.

This doesn't solve the problem of scaling. MacOS still doesn't love the 4K resolution, so you'll need to play around with different resolutions and decide which suits your needs best. When you plug it in, it defaults to a 2560 x 1440 resolution in macOS. This doesn’t yield the same sharpness as running a native 1440p on a Windows machine, but it still looks quite sharp. If you upgrade to a 5K monitor, you won't have to deal with this, but those tend to be more expensive and often aren't available in OLED. The other macOS quirk I ran into was that I could only turn on HDR if I changed the refresh rate to 60 Hz.

Despite the macOS hiccups, the 120-Hz refresh rate is a nice touch in the PA279CDV. It's increasingly common in cheaper monitors, even appearing in the Dell 27 Plus 4K, which is often on sale for less than $300. But it nicely matches the refresh rate of the MacBook Pro and gives the screen smoother animation and motion. And while serious gamers will certainly desire a faster display, 120 Hz at least allows games to look fluid at frame rates over 60 frames per second (fps).

Hope for HDR

There's a lot to like about the PA279CDV and very few reasons for frustration. I'm thrilled to see the category of non-OLED gaming monitors grow, especially in the direction of affordability. The vast majority of laptop screens and monitors lack any meaningful HDR support. So, as these HDR-capable monitors become more accessible, the hope is that we'll see more high-quality HDR content available online. Heck, most browsers and streaming services don't even support HDR at this point. The PA279CDV is exactly what we need more of to improve the situation, and the monitor’s strong port selection makes it a solid option for a home-office workstation in its own right.

Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. He’s been reporting on tech for over a decade, previously at Digital Trends as the senior editor in computing, where he spent seven years leading the publication’s daily coverage. ... Read More

entries.title: Tempo Promo Codes: Get up to 60% Off Healthy Meals
entries.summary: Upgrade your meal prep with these Tempo discount codes and offers. Save on high-protein, ready-to-heat meals delivered to your door.
entries.content:
I had been leery of prepared meal delivery services. They gave me flashbacks to those delivery diet plans sold on late night television in the 1990s. And so Tempo Meals, a spin-off prepared meal brand from meal kit service Home Chef, came as a pleasant surprise even after testing dozens of meal kits.

Tempo meals look like TV dinners, but they’ve never been frozen, thanks to advances in packaging technology. The beef barbacoa and sous-vide chicken I tried actually retained moisture and tenderness. Green beans were still vibrantly green, with a little bit of snap. They’re cooked in a commissary kitchen, and shipped to your doorstep in special packaging that prevents spoilage without using a bunch of preservatives. Heat-and-eat meals won’t ever be quite as good as freshly cooked meals, but especially when I reheated them in an air fryer they got closer than expected.

Tempo is especially known for high-protein and GLP-1 plans created in consultation with dietitians, helping prevent people from losing muscle mass when on calorie-restricted diets or just in midlife. Meals are $11 to $13 a serving at regular price, but Tempo Meals discount codes are available. For now, with a Tempo Meals promo code, you can get up to 60% off your first box of Tempo, with discounts throughout the first month.

Score 30% Off Your First Month of Four Boxes

Like a lot of meal delivery services, Tempo Meals wants you to try them out in hopes you enjoy the service and decide you can’t live without it. And so Home Chef offers a Tempo Meals coupon code for new customers. Depending on the Tempo promo code, this may be a straight discount of 30% off for the first four weeks. Or it may be 50% or 60% off the first box, and then discounts off the next month of boxes. Right now, you can also sign up for a lifetime free breakfast item. For previous customers who for whatever reason paused their Tempo subscription, there are Tempo Meals promo codes for existing customers that show up in your inbox. These may automatically be applied when you visit the Tempo website.

Activate the Heroes Discount to Get 50% Off Now and 10% Off for a Lifetime

Most Tempo Meals promo codes are good for deals during the introductory week only. But the Tempo Meals heroes discount applies for life for military personnel, first responders, teachers, doctors, nurses, and other hospital employees. To get the heroes discount from Tempo, you’ll need to verify your identity with the ID.Me system. After this, you get a permanent discount—pretty much the best discounts available if you plan on using Tempo long-term for a high-protein meal program.

Secure Instant Savings by Applying Your Tempo Meals Coupon

Often, Home Chef offers multiple Tempo Meals coupons at the same time. These can usually be activated on the site by clicking on the right pop-up. After you enter your area code and email address to verify that Tempo serves your area, you’ll be asked a couple questions about your meal preferences, before selecting how many meals you want each week—anywhere from six to 20 meals. At checkout, make sure the right Tempo Meals discount code has been applied to your order. This may include free shipping for the first week, and an extra item such as free breakfast.

entries.title: George Santos Just Got Hit With Kalshi’s First-Ever Lifetime Ban
entries.summary: The former US representative was also fined more than $71,000 for allegedly attempting to manipulate the prediction market.
entries.content:
Former Republican congressman George Santos has received a first-of-its-kind lifetime ban from the prediction market platform Kalshi, which has also fined him $71,356 for violating its rules around insider trading and market manipulation.

According to the notice of disciplinary action Kalshi posted today, the former politician placed trades in markets related to whether he would attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February 2026. He then “began making a series of public statements regarding his attendance at the event in an attempt to influence the price” of certain contracts, some of which were “false or misleading,” per the notice.

The day before the address, Santos posted, “I'm going to be there for the State of Union in the gallery, guys” on X. During the speech, he sent a follow-up noting that he was actually at an airport watching the address on television. “FML,” he wrote.

Kalshi’s enforcement team flagged the trades, froze Santos’ account, and referred the case to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets. This summer, Santos settled with the CFTC for $35,000 over these suspicious trades; a little more than $17,500 was returning the profit he made, with an additional $17,500 fine. At the time, his lawyer issued a statement stressing that Santos settled to “put this matter behind him” and that he had done so “without admitting the Commission’s allegations, findings or conclusions.”

Through his legal representative, Santos declined to comment to WIRED. On social media, however, he had already weighed in, sarcastically thanking Kalshi “for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform,” adding, “Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for 💋,” a nod to the prediction market’s ongoing battles with state authorities over how it is regulated.

Once upon a time, Santos had a rosier relationship with the industry; he was once paid for promoting Kalshi’s rival Polymarket, but Polymarket severed ties with him once federal regulators began looking into his behavior around February’s State of the Union address.

This is far from Santos’ first brush with the law. He was expelled from Congress following an ethics investigation in 2023 and eventually pleaded guilty and served time in federal prison for embezzling from campaign donors, lying to Congress, and defrauding campaign contributors. He was released from prison in 2025 after President Trump commuted his sentence.

According to today’s notice, the prediction market found that Santos successfully influenced the pricing of several markets. Kalshi also issued four additional notices of enforcement actions today, but Santos was the only person penalized who had not settled with the company.

“He wouldn’t talk to us and actively dodged us,” Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana tells WIRED.

In the past year, Kalshi has issued a number of other enforcement actions against politicians whom it found had broken its rules. In this most recent round of enforcement actions, it fined North Carolina congressional candidate Laurie Buckhout, California gubernatorial candidate Stephen Cloobeck, and Maine gubernatorial candidate Ben Midgley for attempting to trade on contracts related to their races; they are all temporarily suspended.

“I bet on myself. Literally. It was a dumb mistake, and as soon as I learned there was an issue, I worked to make it right,” Buckhout, a retired military officer, told WIRED in an email. "Safe to say my career as a Kalshi trader was short-lived.” Cloobeck and Midgley did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Previously, Kalshi fined US Senate candidate Mark Moran for insider trading; at the time, Moran told WIRED that he “did it on purpose” and did not intend to cooperate with Kalshi.

Kalshi’s Diana says that Santos can expect “legal action” if he does not pay.

Updated August 31, 2026, 4:40 pm EDT: This story was updated to correct the spelling of Stephen Cloobeck’s name.

entries.title: Why Food Keeps Making Everybody Sick This Summer
entries.summary: While Trump administration cuts have contributed to the epidemic of foodborne illnesses this summer, there are also deeper issues that make the American food supply chain susceptible to parasites and bacteria outbreaks.
entries.content:
This summer, every meal feels like a risk.

Just as the US is recovering from a major cyclospora outbreak stemming from tainted iceberg lettuce, salmonella has turned up in jalapeños, eggs, and even dog food. The jalapeño-related outbreak is now responsible for at least 431 illnesses and 57 hospitalizations in more than two dozen states. Meanwhile, a dual-pathogen outbreak of E. coli and salmonella linked to alfalfa sprouts has affected 55 people across 15 states.

But is it just your overactive imagination that these outbreaks are worse than normal?

To answer that, WIRED tallied up publicly available numbers from the Food and Drug Administration’s investigations of foodborne illnesses. The agency has identified more than 12,800 illnesses tied to foodborne outbreaks in 2026, already far surpassing the number it has identified in any year since 2020. For comparison, there were 895 cases related to foodborne outbreaks last year.

Experts say the summer of sickness is the result of chronic underfunding in food safety systems, gaps in federal food policy, and recent cuts to the country’s public health infrastructure by President Donald Trump’s administration.

“What is happening this summer just demonstrates to me the vulnerabilities in the system—and what happens when you stress the system,” says Barbara Kowalcyk, director of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition.

To understand how this summer became so swamped with foodborne illnesses, one needs to understand the scale of the cyclospora outbreak, which “was absolutely unprecedented,” says Jennifer McEntire, a food microbiologist and founder of the consulting firm Food Safety Strategy.

The FDA’s numbers, drawn from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s case count, establish this cyclospora outbreak as the largest the agency has investigated in the US since the 1990s. Yet even this figure undercounts how many people actually got sick, according to the CDC’s own calculations.

The FDA’s figures only count illnesses directly linked to a specific outbreak under investigation. So far, about 67 percent of the CDC’s 17,180 laboratory-confirmed cases in the US have been linked to Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce; the rest are linked to other outbreaks or one-off infections, which require a full-blown FDA investigation. On top of that, the CDC is aware of at least 11,844 additional cases that have either not been confirmed by a lab test or require further analysis for other reasons.

Previously, cyclospora infections were rare compared to other common foodborne bugs like salmonella and E. coli. The previously obscure pathogen typically causes a few hundred to a few thousand illnesses a year in the US. Because it is—or at least was—relatively uncommon, cyclospora isn’t included in standard panels that test for several types of gastrointestinal disease. That can mask the true size of an outbreak, on top of the many people who may have gotten diarrhea from the parasite but decided not to go to the doctor.

Cyclospora is also particularly tricky to get rid of, with its tendency to lodge itself into the crevices and folds of leafy greens, herbs, and berries. These foods are typically eaten raw, and food sanitizers aren’t effective at removing the parasite because it forms a tough, protective outer shell.

But the quirks of a parasite cannot fully explain the scale of the outbreak. Last October, WIRED reported that the CDC had reduced its staff through layoffs and buyouts by about 3,000 employees—roughly a quarter of the workforce—since Trump’s second term began. That includes people who worked in a lab that responded to cyclospora outbreaks. According to the team’s former leader, molecular parasitologist Joel Barratt, the lab’s staff was cut from 11 people to just three.

Fewer staff to handle outbreaks is compounded by the nation’s health agencies lacking leadership at the highest levels. The CDC was without a dedicated director for nearly a year, until the Senate voted in early August to confirm Erica Schwartz to the role. The FDA, meanwhile, has not had a permanent commissioner since Marty Makary resigned in May.

In 2025, the Trump administration cut roughly $12 billion in grants for state health departments, which are the first to respond to outbreaks of foodborne illness. In Michigan, the loss of these funds meant 23 fewer infectious disease workers and 123 fewer county health staff, Reuters reported in late July. Health department employees told Reuters they’ve had to pull staff from other areas—and still didn’t have the resources to investigate the thousands of cyclospora cases in the state that’s been at the center of the outbreak.

Putting new food safety policies in place could help prevent large outbreaks, but a traceability rule issued by the FDA in 2022 has yet to be implemented. The rule requires businesses that manufacture, process, pack, or hold leafy greens and other high-risk foods to maintain more detailed recordkeeping. In November, Congress voted to delay implementation of the rule until July 20, 2028. A coalition of food safety and consumer health groups sent a letter to Congress earlier this month urging members to reconsider the delay, saying the rule “would facilitate faster and more effective investigations.”

Even with the new rule, though, outbreaks like the one tied to Taylor Farms lettuce imported from Mexico would be hard to track due to a loophole. De Ann Davis, senior vice president of science at the Western Growers Association, which represents farmers in Arizona, California, Colorado, and New Mexico, says the rule does not apply to importers, brokers, or trading companies that coordinate the movement of food but do not physically possess or handle it.

“In other words, the food can come in without anybody checking that it actually has the necessary traceability information,” she says. “The importer is the one who has to make sure that the food is compliant with those regulations, but they're not subject to the regulations.”

That makes tracing foodborne illness outbreaks tied to foreign products difficult, especially if the original supplier isn’t keeping detailed records. “We are relying on those foreign countries to be informed about the regulations of the US, but they are not subject to the regulations of the US,” Davis says.

There are also lapses in food safety inspections that predate the Trump administration. A January 2025 report from the US Government Accountability Office found that the FDA conducted an average of 917 foreign inspections per year from 2018 to 2023, far fewer than the 8,353 domestic inspections it conducted over the same period. But CBS News reported that inspections have fallen even further since last year’s budget cuts. Taylor Farms’ Mexico facility linked to the cyclospora outbreak has not been inspected since 2019, according to CBS.

In a statement to WIRED, the FDA says that it asked for expanded state and local information sharing, as well as foreign food facility fee collection authority, in its 2027 budget proposal. The agency says that its “robust response” identifying the source of the cyclospora outbreak “demonstrates exactly how the agency's risk-based oversight system is designed to work,” adding that under the Trump administration, the FDA has “increased the number of unannounced foreign inspections and is actively expanding staffing at foreign posts.”

“Suggesting that the FDA's ability to protect the food supply can be measured by a single inspection statistic ignores the agency's comprehensive oversight system,” the statement continues.

Beyond cyclospora, McEntire says the other outbreaks of foodborne illness are still concerning even if they’re smaller in size than the cyclospora crisis. “Multiple visible outbreaks with different organisms associated with very different types of products is kind of unusual, not unprecedented, but certainly unusual,” she says.

Contaminated jalapeños have caused the biggest salmonella outbreak in the US since 2024, when an outbreak of the bacteria in cucumbers caused 551 illnesses that summer. (That’s far below the worst outbreak, though, when an estimated 224,000 people fell ill in 1994 after eating Schwan’s ice cream.)

It’s also rare to find two different disease-causing pathogens in the same product at the same time, which is the case with alfalfa sprouts contaminated with E. coli and salmonella. The outbreak has caused 55 illnesses, with two people getting infected with both pathogens. Everything Sprouts is recalling certain lots of alfalfa sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands at retailers and grocery stores. The sprouts were grown in a hydroponic facility in Minnesota.

Kowalcyk warns that the summer of sickness isn’t over yet, though the calendar is about to turn to fall. Many pathogens thrive in hot, humid environments. Plenty of warm weather is still ahead, and what’s shaping up to be the strongest El Niño on record could jack up temperatures in some locations even further. That means anyone looking for peace of mind at the drive-thru or in the produce aisle after Labor Day may not find it.

“A lot of our foodborne illness cases peak in August, September, even early October,” Kowalcyk says. “So we're just in the beginning.”

entries.title: You Know Who Really Hates AI? Insurance Claims Adjusters
entries.summary: Of the Glassdoor reviews from claims adjusters that mentioned AI, a staggering 98 percent were negative. “AI is just a tool,” one person tells WIRED. “It should never be given the keys.”
entries.content:
On the job review platform Glassdoor, one faction hates artificial intelligence more than any other.

“Pushing AI to the point that you are asking humans not to use their thoughts and brains is such a turn off,” reads one representative review. “Stop forcing AI onto everyone,” reads another. And then there’s this one: “The AI apps this company uses are all trash.”

The reviews in question all come not from journalists or teachers, but from insurance claims adjusters. In fact, recent research from Glassdoor found that claims adjusters who mention AI in their posts are critical a whopping 98 percent of the time—enough to win them the mantle of the biggest AI haters in the American workforce.

Typically, insurance adjusters complain about “AI-obsessed leaders forcing error-prone AI on them and their clients,” according to the research. When AI falls short in this job, adjusters say, they have to clean up a very human mess.

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former insurance claims adjuster who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at khtaylor.24.

Take Ahmad Jackson. About a year ago, he was working in the claims department for a major insurance company. His employer decided to use AI for initial loss reporting, which involves setting up claims and gathering information when someone first discloses an incident. It was supposed to be a boon for employees and policyholders alike, streamlining simple claims while transferring more complex situations to actual people.

Instead, Jackson says, he and other adjusters faced a sudden influx of misclassified claims that required rerouting to the correct department. He encountered AI-driven hallucinations while reading claims summaries; when he inadvertently relayed those errors to claimants or their attorneys, he bore the brunt of their fury.

He quit the company not long after, switching to a different insurance carrier. AI is “getting things wrong,” Jackson tells WIRED. “And it's implementing more work onto the adjusters.”

“There's an AI fatigue,” says Geoffrey Conrad, a claims executive in Mobile, Alabama. “We're pretty much exhausted as far as the amount of AI being shoved down our throats.”

Glassdoor senior economist Chris Martin didn’t expect claims adjusters to hate AI quite this much. When he saw the results, he tells WIRED, he did a double take—then started digging. Martin’s conclusion: The profession is in the midst of a reckoning.

In 2024, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that it expected the number of claims adjusters in the United States to fall by 18,900, or 5 percent, in the coming decade. Between May 2025 and May 2026, employment in the sector dropped a staggering 21 percent, according to BLS data. For early-career adjusters, the decline was even sharper: Entry-level postings have fallen 50 percent since 2025, according to Glassdoor.

The BLS cited technology as a major force behind the decline. In the last few years, AI startups like Liberate and Pace have raised millions of dollars based on promises to “reinvent” insurance, while insurers have scaled their use of AI to handle more and more claims.

In practice, this could look like talking to a chatbot instead of a person to file a claim. Instead of sending people to inspect a damaged home, AI tools might analyze photos or videos to provide estimates for payouts. Hundreds of pages of medical records could be summarized by AI to pull out crucial details. Or an insurer’s AI tool could process a policyholder’s uploaded information—photos, videos, documentation, receipts—then send a payout, all within seconds.

That’s the goal of Lemonade. Since its founding in 2015, the insurance company has promised to replace bureaucracy with “bots and machine learning.” By the end of last year, its proprietary chatbot, AI Jim, handled initial reports 96 percent of the time, with automation handling roughly 55 percent of all claims. While more traditional insurance companies like State Farm emphasize that claims require a mix of human and digital expertise, some claim adjusters still worry they’re training their replacements.

“AI is going to impact many jobs and threaten many incumbents in insurance and the economy,” a Lemonade spokesperson, Paul Staats, tells WIRED, adding that automating allows employees to focus their “empathy, care, and expertise on the most complex claims.”

Glassdoor’s report “should be taken seriously across the industry,” Staats adds.

“There's no jobs, there's no good job prospects,” Martin says. When workers sense layoffs looming, Glassdoor data indicates that their reviews become increasingly anti-AI. Martin says that reviewers also express skepticism about AI when they feel a subpar product is being forced upon them—or upon clients.

Conrad, the Alabama claims adjuster, says people in his profession do feel like they’re being replaced by AI models. “AI is just a tool,” he says. “It should never be given the keys.”

There are instances where AI can make claims adjusters’ lives easier; Jackson says it’s helpful for administrative tasks. He uses it for what he considers “nuisance calls,” like extending someone’s rental car booking by a few days. Justin Tomczak, a representative for State Farm, tells WIRED that the company aims to “give State Farm agents and employees better tools so they can spend more time doing what matters most: helping customers.

But claims adjusters don’t have “a lot of faith in the output,” says Sandy Avina, a claims adjuster turned insurance industry consultant. A smudge in a document from an attorney can result in a hallucination, which leads to an incorrect payout. A missing point in an AI summary of a medical report can do the same. Customers often don’t realize when AI is the root cause of confusion or misinformation, and they assume the adjuster is the one who made the mistake.

Conrad understands that many people see claims adjusters as soulless vultures circling after a catastrophe. But he insists that a good claims adjuster is one who is both empathetic and determined to get the policyholder as much money as possible. He knows, he says, because he’s been there.

Twenty-five years ago, before Conrad started working in the insurance industry, his house burned down. It was a total loss. “If you would have told me that someone was just gonna come take photographs, and an estimate would be generated [by AI] off of photographs, I probably would have lost my mind,” Conrad says.

“I needed somebody to make sure that I'm OK, my family's OK, that we're safe,” Conrad says. AI can be helpful, but not when it’s used as a replacement for humanity. “I think that's a dangerous strategy,” he says.

entries.title: The 9 Best MagSafe Phone Grips for Your Butter Fingers (2026)
entries.summary: Keep your phone firmly in hand and add some personality with these comfortable, durable, and nifty smartphone grips.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The best MagSafe phone grips are basically necessities at this point. Once you start using a grip, it's hard to go back. They just offer such security, especially in this world of phones growing ever larger and sleeker. They can help prevent you from dropping your fancy glass screen on the ground (or worse, on your face), and they also add some visual flair to a device that might otherwise look exactly the same as all the others. The grips often double as kickstands, too—all the better to prop up your phone while you watch YouTube over dinner.

The grips in this guide are designed to be used with Apple's MagSafe technology (or compatible cases, including those for Android). They're easy to take on and off, with a secure hold that stays until you dictate otherwise. We've tested these grips in our day-to-day lives and are always checking out more.

Read our MagSafe guides for additional recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Wallets, Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best 3-in-1 Apple Chargers, and Best iPhone 17 Cases.

Updated August 2026: We've reformatted portions of this guide, checked for accuracy throughout, and added some grips to our new “avoid” section.

What Is MagSafe?

MagSafe is Apple's magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 lineups, as well as the iPhone Air (the iPhone SE and iPhone 16e are excluded). It consists of a ring of magnets on the back of the phone designed for a faster, more precise wireless charging system. But these magnets also opened up the ability to attach different kinds of accessories, like wallets and power banks. It even makes docking an iPhone to a car mount easier.

If you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it comes with MagSafe support (you'll see a ring of magnets on the inside). That way, the MagSafe accessories will have a proper connection. Otherwise, if you use a non-MagSafe case, the accessories will likely slide off due to a weak connection.

If you need a recommendation for a great MagSafe case, we have plenty in our guides:

If you want a magnetic grip, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2, or at least mentions magnets on the product page. All the recommendations here are MagSafe grips.

Can Android Phones Use MagSafe Grips?

Most Android phones are incompatible with MagSafe grips. But there are magnetic cases available for top Android phone models enabling MagSafe-like functionality. You can find WIRED-tested magnetic cases for select Android phones here.

Over the coming years, thanks to the new Qi2 wireless charging standard that incorporates the Magnetic Power Profile, you'll start seeing more high-end Android phones embed magnets inside the device. Google already has Qi2 devices with the Pixel 10 range. That will allow greater compatibility with MagSafe accessories with or without a magnetic case. The road is bumpy, though. Samsung's latest Galaxy S26 range, for example, are “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can only access Qi2 charging speeds and features with a magnet case. Hopefully, manufacturers will add native magnet support soon.

The Different Types of Phone Grips

MagSafe grips are hardly the only type of phone grips available. There are four main other types of grips you can buy.

Cases with attached grips. These are cases with a grip attached to the back. You get a strong and durable grip that will never fall off, but the trade-off is a thicker phone, and these cases typically are incompatible with wireless charging and may not work with other MagSafe accessories.

Clamp-style grips. Also called universal phone grips, these clamp to a phone so you can easily take them on and off, and they're not limited to a particular kind of phone. The downside is they're not the fastest to take on and off, and they can sometimes slide up and down the phone.

Adhesive grips. You can stick a phone grip to the back of your phone or case, and while this will typically give you a well-attached grip that likely won't fall off your phone, the downsides are similar to cases with attached grips. It may block features like wireless charging and restrict you from using other accessories. These grips can also be difficult to remove when you're ready—some have swappable tops, but they don't necessarily allow for easy mixing and matching with different phone cases.

MagSafe grips. These grips are all about convenience. You can easily take them on and off, but they only work with devices or cases with built-in magnets. While you can dangle a phone from a MagSafe grip without issue, additional force could cause the magnets to separate and fling your phone to the ground.

How We Test MagSafe Grips

Each MagSafe grip in this guide is one we used as a primary phone grip for weeks or months at a time. We make sure they snap securely to an iPhone or MagSafe case, and we also ensure they provide a comfortable hold for long periods and are durable enough to withstand drops and heavy use. We use the phone as we normally would—scrolling through social media, FaceTiming with friends, and sending texts and emails—and evaluate the grip to see if it gets in the way or makes life easier.

Other MagSafe Grips We’ve Tested

Spigen OM104 MagSafe Phone Grip: The OM104 is a phone/grip combo accessory for MagSafe and Qi2 devices that comes with a flexible nylon strap to slide your finger through while holding your phone. Dual magnets and a robust metal construction make the OM104 feel like money well spent, and even after hours of sliding my finger in and out of the strap, it still feels soft, flexible, and most importantly, comfortable. It has one annoying design oversight. As you slide your phone in and out of your pocket, the nylon strap will start to droop down. The strap is longer than the grip itself, so when you close the kickstand, it’ll get pinched inside and won’t allow the stand to fully close. It’s comfortable to use, but that quibble knocks it down.

Casely MagRing: Unlike other metal grips we've tested, Casely's MagRing is made of soft silicone. We find it more comfortable on the fingers. It also has a 360-degree swivel, so you can position the grip at virtually any angle. This is strictly a grip, so you can't use it as a kickstand. Since the grip doesn't fold in, your phone won't lie fully flat on a surface. We also tested the MagRing+, which comes with a ring clip for attaching your keys. That comes in handy for quick trips to the grocery store or when you go to the gym and need a place to put your car keys and key fob. But Jacob prefers the standard MagRing, since he typically carries his keys in his pocket or bag. Casely has a few variations of the MagRing and MagRing+ in stock, but it appears to be on its last legs.

Smartish Wallflower: It isn’t perfect, but we still love it. The Smartish Wallflower comes with seven small suction cups that look like a flower, allowing you to attach your phone to a wall (or any other surface) and leave it be. It mostly works, but it largely depends on how heavy your phone is and what surface you’re attaching it to. We didn’t have issues with an iPhone 17 and drywall, but the iPhone 15 Pro Max attached to a particleboard cabinet was too heavy for the grip to manage.

Avoid These MagSafe Grips

OhSnap! Snap Grip: I like that this grip allows you to use other MagSafe accessories, but the point of a MagSafe grip (to me) is that you can remove it easily enough that it doesn't hinder accessories in the first place. So it seems like sort of a needless feature. More importantly, this grip doesn't feel secure to me. I have a harder time keeping a good handle on my phone when I use it, which negates the purpose. The lack of bulk is nice, but a phone ring can provide essentially the same thing with a bit more security. And this grip has a tendency to stick to your accessories rather than your phone when you remove it.

PopSockets Low-Pro Grip and Stand: All phone grip analyses are going to be subjective, but I'm not a fan of how flimsy this new PopSocket feels. It's quite floppy, so I feel like my hand has to do more work to compensate for holding my phone, in which case I'd rather not use a grip in the first place. It's also very difficult to open with one hand. I'm of the mind that accessories shouldn't require more work than you'd need to put in without them. This PopSocket fails that test. Finally, like the OhSnap grip, this sticks to accessories too well. It regularly pulls off or sticks to the car mounts I'm testing rather than sticking to my phone.

entries.title: ATM Flaws Reveal Key Weaknesses in the Software Supply Chain
entries.summary: A security researcher discovered nine vulnerabilities impacting ATM encryption and authentication software. But the problems extend far beyond your local cash machine.
entries.content:
For the past five years, security researcher Matt Burch has immersed himself in the esoteric and high-stakes world of ATM security, in which small software flaws can sometimes expose cold, hard cash. As Burch has bored deeper into the computers powering these digital lock boxes—and continued to find vulnerabilities in key digital security systems—he has started working to raise the alarm, not just about overlooked ATM flaws, but about how that same software used in other industries can introduce weaknesses in an array of critical systems.

At the Black Hat and Defcon security conferences in Las Vegas this month, Burch presented findings about nine vulnerabilities that have been fixed in disk encryption and pre-boot authentication software called CryptoPro Secure Disk. The flaws could have been exploited to bypass CryptoPro's integrity checks and gain full access to encrypted devices.

Made by the German software firm CryptWare, CryptoPro is marketed to ATM makers and is used in some ATMs, including as part of Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Suite. But CryptoPro is also sold as a security solution for other embedded-device makers, as well as big organizations using Microsoft Windows, underscoring the supply chain challenge of addressing bugs when software is widely implemented in numerous industries.

“ATMs are what brought me down this path, but I think there may be an even higher impact of these findings beyond that,” Burch says. “From the perspective of ATMs and the financial network, there are a lot of layers, and I think as a result of that, things just get implemented a certain way and then there’s limited technical insight—bugs can get overlooked or they don’t get addressed.”

CryptWare managing director Uwe Saame tells WIRED that the company patched the nine bugs in two phases with CryptoPro version 7.7.2 in early November and 7.7.3 in early December. He adds that there are hundreds of CryptoPro customers across critical industries including “automotive, banking, government agencies, manufacturing, research, finance, and healthcare. There are also extensive installations in the ATM sector.”

Burch says the company was prompt and collaborative throughout his disclosure process and he validated that the patches actually fix the vulnerabilities he found.

While CryptoPro does not publicly release update notes, Saame says that the company has maintenance agreements with all customers and notifies them in advance about any security findings as well as the company's timeline for resolving them. “As a rule, the new version is already available to our customers before its official publication,” he says.

Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson Michael Jacobsen tells WIRED in a statement that only two of the nine vulnerabilities are relevant to Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Hard Disk Encryption, the system where the ATM maker uses CryptoPro software. Jacobsen says that Diebold Nixdorf issued fixes related to those two bugs in December, but that they could not have been exploited on their own to compromise a Diebold Nixdorf ATM.

In ATMs, embedded devices, and enterprise security more broadly, the challenge of the software supply chain comes from all of the steps to actually apply fixes in the world. As in this case, a developer has to release a patch, then companies that implement the product in their own software need to develop a tailored fix, and then customers need to actually hear about and install that patch—which can be difficult for systems that are running in the field or can't easily be paused and updated.

Speaking generally about this challenge, Jacobsen, the Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson, says that “when a security issue is identified, Diebold Nixdorf assesses the impact, identifies affected products and configurations, and develops any needed updates through our product security and engineering processes. We then notify impacted customers and provide updates through standard software distribution channels, including the Global Security Portal where applicable. For deployed ATMs, updates are coordinated with each customer based on their operating model, service agreements, and change-management processes.”

Security researchers have warned for decades about the danger of relying on “security through obscurity” by trying to hide software from view or keep it locked away. And, as a result of this work, internet-of-things manufacturers and those in critical industries like the financial sector and medical device manufacturing have made some progress on transparency and promoting patch adoption. But Burch points out that as AI systems make it easier to evaluate software and find vulnerabilities—even for researchers or attackers who don't have granular expertise in a given area—it is more pressing than ever to shed light on niche security products.

“AI really blows away the obscurity model,” Burch says. “You don’t need to fully understand how something works anymore to move forward and potentially have a big impact.”

Updated 8/31/2026 at 8 am EDT: Added additional details from CryptoWorks.

entries.title: Google Maps Now Shows ‘Lake America’ Instead of Lake Ontario
entries.summary: After Donald Trump’s executive order demanding the name change, Google is the first major online map provider to flip the switch.
entries.content:
Lake Ontario is no more on Google Maps in the US. Google changed the name of the easternmost of the Great Lakes to “Lake America” late Saturday, days after President Donald Trump ordered its rebranding in official government databases.

Trump issued the executive order on Thursday as part of an ongoing feud over tariffs with Canada, whose province of Ontario borders the lake. It followed a similar order he issued in January 2025 to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America as part of a fight with the US trading partner to the south.

Google, Apple, Microsoft, and other maps providers adopted the Gulf of America naming as soon as the US Department of the Interior updated its records, which came a couple of weeks after Trump’s order. So it was no surprise that when those records—which are used to determine names on roadway signs and in government literature—reflected Lake America, digital maps from Google also quickly took on the new name.

Apple Maps and Bing Maps have not yet reflected the change but are expected to. In fact, the map for the federal government’s Geographic Names Information System database, which informs these changes, still showed Lake Ontario as of Sunday morning, with a note that the maps are “in the process of being updated to reflect this name change.”

While Google and other private organizations that provide maps are not bound by law to use official names, they generally follow government databases like GNIS. The location names a user sees depends on their own geography.

“People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in an unsigned statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.”

Trump’s efforts to rewrite maps have generated considerable public debate in open-source mapping communities such as OpenStreetMap, whose technology is used by companies such as Uber and Lyft. Ultimately, OpenStreetMap recognizes both the US and foreign names and gives organizations using its maps the choice over which to show.

One map provider that has so far declined to make the change is MapQuest, which said in a social media post in response to Trump’s order, “We’re not changing it.”
